🚨 🇺🇲 The US bond market is starting to say the trillions of dollars promised to build its infrastructure could become impossible to finance under current conditions and I think we are witnessing a genuine regime shift.

📊 For three years, markets have rewarded companies announcing the most spectacular investment plans, but now investors are finally starting to ask the right questions. Who is financing these projects? At what cost? With what guarantees? For what return? 47 major data center projects have been delayed, canceled, or blocked in 2026, while only 35% of the US data center pipeline is actually credible according to Bernstein. We are talking about a potential investment wave exceeding $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032 - FT

📉 Companies developing these infrastructures must spend billions upfront to purchase GPUs, build data centers and secure electricity supplies, while the associated revenues may not materialize for several years. Their entire business model depends on their ability to keep raising capital at reasonable costs, but that assumption is currently being challenged. CoreWeave lost 25% last week while some of its bonds suffered a sharp sell-off as the market is wondering whether these projects are financially viable at all.

➡️ Few other examples to understand. Cipher agreed to absorb the first $359 million in cost overruns on one project, creating an additional equity requirement of $750 million. Nscale has a contract potentially worth $45 billion with Anthropic but Anthropic can walk away if certain financing or delivery commitments are not met. Meanwhile, SB Energy needs around $174 billion in capital to fulfill contracts representing $430 billion in future revenue, despite not having completed a single data center. Some companies are being valued on enormous contracts without having demonstrated that they can actually finance and deliver the infrastructure behind them.

⚠️ We also need to revisit the circular financing structure of this industry which I have discussed before. Nvidia invests in companies that buy its chips, AI labs sign contracts that allow developers to raise debt, and SPVs or private credit funds finance infrastructure based on expected future revenues. As long as capital keeps flowing, the system works, but if investors suddenly demand much higher yields, the entire mechanism can start breaking down. Projects get delayed, GPU orders are postponed, developers face financial difficulties, and creditors reassess their exposure. A financing crisis can trigger an investment crisis before demand for AI even starts slowing down and many people tend to forget that. Moreover, that risk is concerning given how important AI-related investment has become as a driver of US economic growth.

📈 I do not think we are witnessing the collapse of the entire industry. Instead, we may be entering a much more brutal selection process between financially viable projects and those built on unrealistic assumptions. Lower Fed rates will not solve the problem as if credit spreads widen faster than risk-free rates decline, the overall cost of financing will continue to rise.

💸 I maintain that we need to return to a cost of capital and valuation levels that are consistent with the actual economic profitability of these projects. The technological success of AI does not guarantee financial success for the companies funding its infrastructure. History has already taught us this through railroads, telecommunications, and the internet. A technology can revolutionize the economy while destroying enormous amounts of investor capital.

The current tensions in the bond market are a serious warning sign ⚠️

⚒️ DAILY METALS PULSE — WEEKEND EDITION
Sunday, 18 October 2026

Floating reactors buying uranium. Old mine stockpiles delivering fresh value. China accelerating gold purchases.

Four developments worth a closer look:

☢️ URANIUM — A new customer is securing fuel

Bluecore Energy announced the purchase of low-enriched uranium this week for its floating nuclear development programme, following a $50 million seed financing.

The material still needs fuel fabrication, and deployment remains ahead. But this is an actual uranium purchase from a developer moving toward testing.

What interests me: maritime nuclear is beginning to translate engineering ambitions into fuel procurement. Another potential source of future demand to follow.

🥈 SILVER — The interesting detail inside Aya’s record quarter

$AYA reported record quarterly production of 2.03 million silver-equivalent ounces, up 51% year over year.

Roughly 26% came from reclaiming historical pyrite stockpiles at Boumadine. Meanwhile, Zgounder itself delivered record silver production of approximately 1.50 million ounces.

There is value in material already sitting above ground. The distinction matters, though: that stockpile contribution has a limited life. Sustained growth still requires sustained mine performance.

🔌 COPPER — A strike ends; the bigger challenge remains

Sunday’s fresh development: workers ratified an agreement ending the Centinela strike in Chile. Antofagasta said production had remained normal, so the immediate change is reduced disruption risk.

The longer-term warning came from Teck’s CEO on Thursday: he sees a potential 2035 supply shortfall equivalent to around 30 tier-one mines.

That is his forecast, but it illustrates the scale of investment copper may require.

🥇 GOLD — China’s buying accelerated during a pullback

Thursday’s World Gold Council update showed China added 23 tonnes to official gold reserves in September, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023.

That brought Q3 purchases to 63 tonnes. Chinese gold ETF holdings also reached a month-end record of 304 tonnes.

Official buying and investment demand strengthened even as prices retreated. Jewellery demand remains weaker, making the identity of the buyer particularly interesting.

👀 NEXT WEEK

I’m watching copper’s reaction to the Chile settlement, the direction of US bond yields, and miners’ production updates. Fuel procurement, durable output and reserve accumulation remain central to my metals thesis.

Crypto prompt of the day:

You're valuing a crypto token the way a good equity analyst values a company: from the cash it actually returns to its owners. Most token valuations borrow a P/E from other tokens, which just imports their mispricing. This one derives the multiple from the protocol's own economics, so every number traces back to a source or a stated assumption. I'll use your report to decide what I believe, so being honest about what's known matters more than looking precise.

Start by asking which token I mean (and the chain, if the name is ambiguous). Ask whether I can share DefiLlama screenshots, docs links or recent buyback or unlock news. Tell me it's all optional and you'll research anything I don't send. Cite a source and date for every figure you use. If you can run code, do the maths in code.

How to build the valuation:

**Earnings (E0).** Count only the cash that reaches token holders: DefiLlama's "holders revenue" (buybacks, burns and payouts). Fees mostly go to liquidity providers and builders, so they overstate what holders get. Holder revenue is already the holders' share, so don't apply a payout ratio on top.
- **A year or more of history:** use the last 12 months.
- **30 days to a year:** use the lower of the 90-day and 14-day rates, annualised, then cap it at what the last 14 days of protocol revenue can fund. Young tokens' early numbers usually fade, and buybacks can lag a fall in revenue.
- **Under 30 days:** too little to value.
- **Nothing reaches holders yet:** value it only if a real mechanism exists (a governance proposal, or paused buybacks), and lead with the value if it switched on today.

**Supply.** Count every token with a claim on that cash: circulating, vested but unclaimed, scheduled vesting, and part of the unissued emissions pool, released evenly with 75% out by year 7. How much of the pool depends on discipline:
- if the team holds the largest single allocation and the protocol funds itself from fees, count 60 / 10 / 0% (bear / base / bull);
- otherwise count 100 / 60 / 10%.

Show both, because this one choice can move the value by 15–20%.

**Growth (g1, years 1–7, to the nearest 5%).**
- **Base and bull:** g1 = (reset × (1 + market growth)^6 × share change)^(1/7) − 1.
  - Market growth (base) is a third of the category's multi-year growth, capped at ±20%. Bull adds 10 points; bear takes 10 off.
  - The reset is 0.6522 × (record 12-month level ÷ current level), at most 1, so a past boom isn't extrapolated.
  - The share change is ×1.25 (base) or ×1.5 (bull) for a strong moat, ×1.0 or ×1.25 otherwise.
- **Bear:** the bear market growth.
- **No category history, or a young category that's shrinking:** market growth 0%.
- **Perps exchanges:** total market data isn't free, so use 61% trailing growth, a 0.6522 reset, and an extra factor for the on-chain share of perps rising from 7% to 10 / 30 / 35%.

**Return on equity (ROE), from the moat.** Growth only adds value while returns stay above the cost of capital.
- Near-monopoly: 55 / 75 / 100%.
- Strong (category leader, real network effects, 18+ months old): 35 / 50 / 70%.
- Moderate: 25 / 35 / 40%.
- Weak or easily copied: 10 / 15 / 20%.

Never use an ROE below the terminal cost of equity.

**Cost of equity (Ke), built from the risks.** Add up:
- the US 10-year Treasury yield;
- Damodaran's US equity risk premium;
- regulation:
  - no KYC with unresolved US exposure: 2.5 / 2.0 / 0.5%;
  - past US probes closed: 1.0%;
  - regulated: 0.5%;
- governance: 0.4% for each of concentrated control, a team that can change the rules, and no legal wrapper;
- alignment: 0% if buybacks are automatic, 1% if governance controls them, 2% if discretionary;
- smart-contract risk: 2% at launch, falling evenly to 0.5% at three years old.

Jeff drank a bit too much of his own Kool-Aid in this recent Odd Lots clip. I think it's important to clear up a distinction that makes all the difference.

Democratizing access to wealth creation is NOT the same as democratizing access to speculation.

Many of us genuinely want broader participation in attractive investment opportunities. The growing wealth inequality produced by the current system is tearing at the seams of society, something I've spoken about many times.

But let's be clear: listing pre-IPO perpetual futures does absolutely nothing to democratize the wealth being created in private markets.

I've seen this misleading narrative pushed repeatedly by perp DEXs lately, and it needs to be called out.

A pre-IPO perp creates ZERO underlying wealth. It's a zero-sum contract before costs, and negative-sum after them. No capital flows to the company. No ownership changes hands. No new economic opportunity is created.

Every long has a short. There is no free lunch in simply going long something before its IPO, and funding costs can even determine the outcome more than any price moves. TRADING access is NOT INVESTING access.

In fact, in many ways pre-IPO perps are almost the antithesis of democratized access:

They create the illusion of participation in private-market wealth creation, while actually offering retail a speculative instrument whose mechanics they are often poorly equipped to understand.

The result is a playground for the FEW sophisticated traders who understand funding, oracle design, and liquidation mechanics to extract value from the MANY who don't.

To give credit where it's due, Robinhood's efforts toward sourcing actual employee shares, placing them into SPVs, and tokenizing genuine spot ownership are much closer to meaningful democratization.

That can unlock real economic value by allowing employees to exchange some of their expected upside for liquidity, while giving new investors actual economic exposure. A legitimate financial trade-off, without the funding-rate and liquidation shenanigans.

I'm strongly aligned with expanding access to investment opportunities. And I believe advances in AI and blockchain can dramatically lower the barriers to discovering, structuring, and distributing them.

But let's not BS ourselves that launching another zero-sum casino contract is moving the needle on wealth inequality.

What would actually move the needle is bringing real capital formation and ownership onchain. Giving investors access to productive, illiquid assets like data centers, GPUs, and select startup investing, where capital can actually finance growth and share in the resulting value creation.

These opportunities are harder to structure, underwrite, and bring to market, and we haven't seen many compelling implementations onchain yet. 

Hopefully this will change soon and, as the industry matures, we can direct more of our energy toward actually expanding access to wealth creation.

There’s nothing like a Sunday for discussing current market conditions. And that’s exactly what we’re going to do today.

When we encounter a difficult situation, we like to categorize it.

For example, is this a problem that money can solve? Or, more relevant to the current situation, can we learn something from it and draw useful lessons?

That is what we’ll explore here.

The world’s leading pharmaceutical and biotech analyst is Umer Raffat, who works in New York for Evercore ISI.

As we do every weekend, we listened to his weekly podcast. This time, he opened with the topic of fund performance.

Here are a few things we learned.

First, the chaos in fund performance is not limited to biotech. According to ISI, technology funds are also going through a difficult and chaotic period.

This suggests that the current situation may also be connected to rising interest rates, in addition to the performance of $MRNA, a subject we have discussed extensively before.

Within biotech, ISI reports that market-neutral funds are down approximately 2% this year, while long-biased funds are down by double digits, except for a few fortunate funds that held stocks involved in M&A transactions.

Just how chaotic is the situation?

We have already seen junk stocks, led by $MRNA, skyrocket.

At the same time, large pharmaceutical stocks have rallied strongly, benefiting from a flight to safety.

The DRG index has gained approximately 15% over the past year and around 4% since the beginning of October.

To illustrate the chaos, we asked Claude to examine the 13F filings of the 25 largest dedicated healthcare hedge funds and identify their 25 most popular holdings.

We then asked Claude to chart the performance of these stocks this year.

The results show a 32.3% decline over the past month and a half.

Making matters worse, many healthcare funds also held significant short positions in stocks that surged dramatically, including $MRNA, $GRAL, $TWST, $IOVA, $NTRA, and others.

Naturally, this intensified the pain.

So, is the lesson to avoid popular stocks?

Not necessarily.

Even high-quality, attractively valued companies outside the market consensus have experienced aggressive selling.

It appears that investors have been selling quality stocks to chase speculative biotech names and large pharmaceutical companies.

One important lesson is that hedging through the $XBI ETF, which has substantial exposure to speculative biotech stocks, has provided relatively little protection against this particular market rotation.

What happens next?

One way to evaluate the opportunity is through forward valuations.

Using projected 2031 earnings, certain high-quality biotech companies appear to trade at significant discounts to the broader pharmaceutical industry.

An important distinction is that many of these companies have already successfully completed Phase 3 clinical trials or reached more advanced stages of development.

There are also numerous potential acquisition candidates, including:

$MDGL, $CELC, $COGT, $ABVX, $MLYS, $CGON, $BBIO, $MLTX, $PRAX, $PCVX, $BMRN, $CTMX, $GERN, $IONS, $NBIX, $CYTK, $TVTX, $SNDX, $SVRA.

Another attractive characteristic of some of these companies is that they may not need additional capital to reach profitability.

This distinction could become increasingly important if access to capital becomes more difficult.

The investment conclusion

Given these conditions, there appears to be little logic in selling high-quality, attractively valued mid-cap biotech companies simply to chase speculative stocks or large pharmaceutical companies trading at historically elevated multiples.

In fact, the current environment may offer an opportunity to establish or increase exposure to high-quality, mid-cap biotech value stocks.

In times like this, if you're a long term investor, you don't want to be waffling about being in or out, you want to be stacking units systematically. Don't get confused by the traders, it's a separate game.

On unit accumulation, depending on how long you've been in the game, it's helpful to think in "relative units" of the investment you did best with. I'll use $ETH because the math is easy and relates well to younger networks. 

ETH has ~120M units. Let's say I once held 10 ETH.

Now I'm looking to stack $SOL, but SOL has ~636M units, or ~5.3x the # of units. Therefore, to have an equivalent position size in network terms, I'd need 53 SOL. If I want to own double the network % of SOL, that I owned of ETH, I'd need 106 SOL.

Or, perhaps I'm considering $TIA, which has ~1.16B total supply, or ~9.7x the # of units of ETH. In that case, I'd need 97 units of TIA to have a network equivalent. If I want to place a bigger network bet on TIA, because the network value is lower than when I entered ETH, then 10x the % ownership would require me to accumulate 970 TIA. 100x the % ownership = 9,700 TIA. Going for significantly more ownership, at cheap prices, if you're right, can lead to asymmetric outcomes.

$ZEC is another good example of this, since its supply mirrors $BTC's. And so it's easy to think of your "dream # of BTC," and aim to accumulate that in ZEC, if you're so inclined.

Pick your networks of choice, and do the math. I have always found thinking in unit terms keeps me grounded, optimistic, and goal oriented in dreary times. I can then dream about future upside in the thick of the bull, but the important thing is to systematically stack the units with a high conviction methodology in the bear or early-bull pullbacks. 

In terms of where we are now, which is probably why most of you are still reading :) BTC has been bleeding out the long-tail while remaining resilient, with many names 20-40%+ down from the highs while BTC is down just shy of 10%. You can either say BTC has already bled the risk appetite out of the market and so most of the work is done, or you can say BTC hasn't dropped much so it'll be really terrible if it goes cliff diving. I'm sympathetic to the former view. 

I read this as an early-bull opportunity rather than a warning sign that this move was a "bull trap," and so I'm inclined to be a buyer. You have to respect the possibility of lower levels, and so tranche out any dry powder that remains with % cash used corresponding to % probability those levels are the local bottom - yes, you likely end up with some excess cash if not all levels are hit, but that's okay. And don't forget, there's already opportunity in front of you.
